issues.legal_issue: A court may recall an earlier order obtained by fraud even after a special leave petition challenging that order has been dismissed.
material_facts: The State sought recall of an earlier High Court order after special leave petitions challenging that order had been dismissed.
The High Court considered a CBI report and other material indicating that the landowners and officials had misled the authorities about possession of the land.
The Supreme Court accepted that the earlier order was liable to be recalled because of the fraud found by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal of the special leave petitions did not prevent the High Court from recalling its earlier order in the circumstances, because the order was alleged and found to have been procured by fraud.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136, dismissal of a petition for special leave does not ordinarily attract the doctrine of merger; the order below is not replaced by the Supreme Court's refusal of leave. Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala explains this distinction and considers Abbai Maligai Partnership Firm v. K. Santhakumaran. In any event, fraud is an exception: an order procured by fraud is a nullity and cannot be allowed to stand. The Court also relied on the fraud principles in Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley, S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd. and United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh.

predicates.recall_application: A party applied to the court that made an earlier order to have that order recalled.
predicates.special_leave_petition_refused: A petition seeking permission to appeal against the earlier order was refused without the matter proceeding as an appeal.
predicates.fraud_materially_misled_the_court: A party's deliberate deception materially misled the court when it made the earlier order.

issues.definition: When an application seeks recall after a special leave petition has been refused and material fraud misled the court, the earlier order may be recalled.

issues.legal_issue: A judicial order obtained by fraud is a nullity and may be challenged in later proceedings.
material_facts: The High Court found that material facts about possession had been misrepresented or suppressed in proceedings concerning the land.
The Supreme Court considered the effect of fraud on the validity and finality of judicial orders.
issues.conclusion: An order obtained by fraud is non-existent in law and may be challenged in any court, including in collateral proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Fraud vitiates judicial acts and defeats the ordinary principle of finality. The Court relied on Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley; S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, which requires litigants to approach the court with clean hands and disclose material documents; Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd., which recognises the court's inherent power under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to recall an order obtained by fraud on the court; and United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh, which recognises recall where newly discovered fraud affects the basis of an order.

predicates.judicial_order_at_issue: A party asks a court to give effect to or reconsider an order made in judicial proceedings.
predicates.order_obtained_by_fraud: A party procured the order through deliberate deception that affected the court's decision.

issues.definition: If a judicial order was procured through deception affecting the decision, the order is a nullity.

issues.legal_issue: Land remains includible in a declarant's holdings for urban land ceiling purposes when land acquisition proceedings have not been completed, even if possession is said to have been transferred for the acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners asserted that possession had been handed over to a public authority before the urban land ceiling law came into force.
The record indicated that tenants occupied the land and that neither the landowners nor the public authority had actual or physical possession.
Land acquisition proceedings had not been completed and no award had been passed.
The competent authority had treated the landowners as having no surplus land on the basis that possession had already been transferred.
issues.conclusion: The land was subject to the urban land ceiling law and should not have been excluded from the landowners' holdings merely because possession was said to have been handed over for an acquisition that had not been completed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Because the acquisition proceedings had not been completed and no award had been passed, title remained with the landowners; any possession held by the acquiring authority was, in law, for the landowners. The competent authority therefore could not exclude the land on the basis of the asserted transfer of possession.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_determination: An authority is determining whether land is surplus under an urban land ceiling regime.
predicates.land_title_remained_with_declarants: The declarants retained legal title to the land.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_uncompleted: Proceedings to acquire the land had not reached completion and no final award had been made.

issues.definition: When an urban land ceiling determination concerns land still legally owned by the declarants and acquisition remains incomplete, the land must be included in their holdings.

issues.legal_issue: Suo motu revisional power with no prescribed limitation period must be exercised within a reasonable time, assessed in light of the circumstances and when material facts became known.
material_facts: The original order declaring that there was no surplus land was made in 1981.
A public authority's 1985 letter stated that it had not taken actual physical possession because tenants remained on the land.
The State initiated revision proceedings after that information emerged and ultimately set aside the original order in 1995.
The record also contained later communications and material indicating possible collusion and fraud.
issues.conclusion: In the circumstances, the State's exercise of suo motu revisional power was not shown to have occurred after an unreasonable period.
issues.legal_principle: Although Section 34 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 prescribed no limitation period for the State's suo motu revision, the power had to be exercised within a reasonable time. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Raghav Natha and assessed reasonableness in light of the circumstances, including when the relevant information came to light and the subsequent developments.

rule.if: suo_motu_revision_case and no_fixed_revision_deadline and revision_followed_discovery_of_material_facts and delay_explained_by_case_circumstances

predicates.suo_motu_revision_case: A public authority initiated revision of its own motion rather than on an application by a party.
predicates.no_fixed_revision_deadline: The governing framework set no specific time limit for exercising the revisional power.
predicates.revision_followed_discovery_of_material_: The authority initiated revision after receiving information that materially called the original decision into question.
predicates.delay_explained_by_case_circumstances: The history of the matter and later developments provided an explanation relevant to the period before revision was exercised.

issues.definition: When suo motu revision has no fixed deadline, follows discovery of material facts, and the delay is explained by the circumstances, the revision may be treated as timely.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not interfere under Article 136 with a High Court's recall order where the record supports serious fraud allegations and no miscarriage of justice is shown.
material_facts: The High Court recalled its earlier order and directed the authorities to reconsider the matter after providing the parties an opportunity to be heard.
A CBI report and other material supported serious allegations that the earlier proceedings had been affected by fraud.
The Supreme Court clarified that it was not deciding the underlying merits of the land ceiling or acquisition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere under Article 136 and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers discretionary and equitable power rather than a right of appeal, and the Supreme Court intervenes where justice requires it. The Court referred to Baiganna v. Deputy Collector of Consolidation and held that the record did not disclose a miscarriage of justice requiring intervention.

predicates.article_136_appeal: A party asks the Supreme Court to exercise its discretionary special appellate jurisdiction over a lower court's order.
predicates.high_court_recalled_order_on_fraud_mater: The High Court recalled an earlier order after considering material supporting allegations that fraud affected it.
predicates.no_miscarriage_of_justice_shown: The circumstances do not establish an injustice requiring the Supreme Court to intervene.

issues.definition: When an Article 136 appeal challenges a recall order supported by material indicating fraud and no miscarriage of justice is shown, the Supreme Court declines to interfere.
